newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan overall trade surplus falls, but up with US.
newsitem.headline: Japan overall trade surplus falls, but up with US.

text.p: Japan's overall trade surplus fell for a 23rd straight month in October but that with the United States increased for the first time in 20 months, due mainly to a pickup in car exports, the Finance Ministry said on Monday.

The overall surplus fell 12.9 percent from a year earlier to 470.86 billion yen ($4.24 billion) while the surplus with the United States, which is often a source of trade friction, rose 31.3 percent to 354.79 billion yen ($3.19 billion).
The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.

A Finance Ministry official told reporters that the figures showed the overall surplus was still declining and added that he did not think the declining trend in the surplus with the United States had changed, despite October's figures.

Private economists had estimated an overall surplus of between 396 billion yen ($3.56 billion) and 650 billion yen ($5.85 billion) against a 540.5 billion yen ($4.86 billion) surplus a year ago and a 779.52 billion yen ($7.02 billion) surplus in September.
According to MOF data, the increase in the surplus with the United States was mainly due to a rise in car exports, which grew 44.4 percent from a year ago.
"What you see here is that the rise in the trade surplus with the U.S. is almost entirely due to the cutback of reverse imports," said Jesper Koll, chief economist of JP Morgan in Tokyo.
"Japanese carmakers are now substituting U.S. products with Japanese products to meet Japanese demand. That is really the driving force here.

"This (the overall trade surplus decline) is a fortunate number for Japan in the short term, but longer term, what we are seeing in the U.S.-Japan trade balance is signalling a rise in the global surplus down the road."
Yasushi Okuda, an economist at BZW in Tokyo, said the increase in the car exports to the United States was partly due to the fact the strong yen a year ago meant exports then were extremely weak.
A drop in the yen makes Japanese products cheaper in terms of foreign currency and vice versa.
Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute, said although the surplus had now been in decline for almost two years, the situation was now different.
"It's almost a flat situation, or a little bit of a downward situation compared with a year earlier," he said.
"There is the structural change of trade, that is the shift of production from Japan to overseas, where we see a huge inflow of foreign goods from Asian countries and the United States continuing.

"The structural trend (of a declining trade surplus) is continuing. But at the same time, the foreign-exchange effect, that is the cheaper yen, will have an effect on Japanese exports. So in the near future, we will see a so-called "bottoming-out" phenomenon of the trade surplus.

"This new situation of the trade figures will start a stronger Japanese yen in the near future. My prediction is that the Japanese yen will be going between 103 and 113 yen against the U.S. dollar until the end of the next fiscal year.
The yen was trading at about 111 to the dollar on Monday morning.
